V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01220
The Book is precisely this revelation from the Lord of the worlds as it descends (tanzil) into a form accessible to us.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01221

The distinction between the world of the divine Command ('alam al-amr) and the created world ('alam al-khalq) is fundamental to Islamic esoteric thought. Broadly speaking, the world of the Command receives its existence directly and eternally from God's command “Be!” (Esto, KN). The created world, by contrast, comes into being through the world of the Command, which stands between it and that first creative act.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01222

We have already seen how Shiite thinkers explain this distinction while avoiding confusion about the unity of being (wahdat al-wujud)—the idea that being has one and the same meaning wherever it is found. In the account given above, that unity begins only at the second spiritual level, or maqam. There we are already dealing with being brought into existence. The act that brings something into existence—the active divine Command (amr fi'li)—remains beyond being itself, beyond the very existence it commands into being. That existence is the receiving side of the Command, what Latin philosophers called its significatio passiva.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01223

For the Illuminationist philosophers, the world of pure Intelligences is the world of the Command. Our Shiite thinkers agree, but with an important qualification: this is the Command as received and brought into effect (amr maf'uli). In that sense, the Intelligences are already created beings.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01224

Yet they do not belong to the created world called 'alam al-khalq. Their creation is eternal; it does not enter ordinary chronological time. Their time is not ours, but the “subtle time” discussed earlier by Qazi Sa'id Qummi. The pure Intelligences receive the eternal Command directly and embody its effect, just as iron placed in fire receives its heat and becomes hot. This is why they can be called the world of the Command, even though they are the Command in its received, or activated, form.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01225
Beneath this difficult vocabulary lies a philosophical decision with far-reaching consequences. The world of Intelligence is often called the First Emanation of the Light of Lights.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01226

But we have also seen that, for Shiite spiritual philosophy, the First Emanation is the Light of Lights itself. It comes directly from the mystery of the Command—the “secret still wrapped in the secret.” This Light of Lights (Nur al-anwar) is the primordial Muhammadan Reality. From it, as the image of the Throne and its four lights suggests, the many levels of spiritual worlds unfold, all the way down to the world we can perceive with our senses.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01227

The way these worlds unfold mirrors the spiritual levels (maqamat) described earlier. Each level marks a successive place where the prophetic Word, or Logos, appears. As the Word passes from one world to the next, it takes on new forms until it becomes the revealed Book in our visible world. For Shiite thinkers, this process already contains the beginnings of both the teaching about prophecy and the teaching about the Imams. That is because the primordial Muhammadan Reality (Haqiqat Muhammadiya) is both what descends and what makes the descent possible.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01228

The Prophet's and the Imams' sayings about hidden meaning all invite us to explore this theme. One famous saying of the Prophet speaks of seven depths of inner meaning; we shall examine a fourteenth-century spiritual writer's treatment of it later (Book IV, Chapter II). Semnani's reading of the “seven prophets of your being” rests on a related insight (see also Book IV, Chapter IV).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01229

To keep our discussion manageable, I shall draw mainly on Sayyed Kazem Reshti's great, unfinished commentary on the Verse of the Throne (Ayat al-Kursi, Qur'an 2:256). Its introduction also uses the two-part saying of Imam Ja'far that we examined in the previous section.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01230

Shiite esoteric thought seeks the true meaning of divine revelations—the hidden meaning within the words. To say what that meaning is, therefore, is also to give some account of how it comes into existence. That brings us back to the successive appearances of the divine Word in different worlds. It also brings us to prophecy and the Imams. The “eternal Imam”—not any individual Imam considered simply as a historical person—holds the secret of the prophetic revelation in every world, because in a profound sense he is that secret. This is extremely difficult to put into words.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01231
Yet it is precisely what the idea of the primordial Muhammadan Reality is meant to express.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01232

We should keep one thing firmly in mind. At every level at which we consider this primordial Reality—the complete spiritual company of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—the Imams exist before earthly history as the “place of the prophetic message.” That, as we saw, is how the Ziyarat al-jami'a first greets them. They are the place where the prophetic Word appears.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01233

At the level of the “secret still wrapped in the secret,” they are the “secret of that secret”: the inner meaning of the inner meaning, concealed within the first manifestation of God. At the next level, they are the “hidden secret” within the appearance of the Muhammadan Word: the inner meaning of its outward form. This is the “secret that only a secret can teach.” The meaning is that no one knows the secret of prophetic revelation unless the Imam shares it with them—and the Imam is himself that secret.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01234
Finally, it is the secret concealed within the visible, literal text of the Book as it appears in our world.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01235

This means that the prophetic Word, the “Messenger of God,” appears across a series of worlds arranged in levels. Every new appearance also involves a concealment, as when the first level gives way to the second. What was outwardly visible at one level becomes hidden at the level below it. The secret underlying these appearances therefore has a distinct way of existing at each level.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01236

From the very beginning, every appearance of the Prophet is inseparable from the Imam and the Imam's secret. Muhammad himself is reported to have said of Ali—that is, of the Imam—“He was sent secretly with every prophet, but with me he was sent openly.” This is why one branch of Shiite interpretation asks how the Imams exist at the different levels where the prophetic Word appears, in worlds that precede our material world. There the Word is still pure speech, before it becomes the Book and takes on the Book's outward, written form. This is also among the hardest questions in Shiite spiritual philosophy, and its thinkers usually address it with great reserve.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01237

What are these different worlds? And how are they represented through the successive levels of the primordial Muhammadan Reality? The answer comes in symbols, especially the image of the Throne ('arsh) in Shiite accounts of creation. Philosophers speak of four fundamental realities: Intelligence ('aql), Spirit (ruh), Soul (nafs), and Nature (tabi'at). Here all four belong to the primordial Muhammadan Reality, the first being brought into existence and the Light of Lights. Four archangels, or four Lights, shine out from this Light of Lights. Each becomes the source of an entire world, which in turn contains other worlds.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01238

The Intelligence of the Muhammadan Reality is the source of every intelligence. Its symbol is white light, the upper pillar on the right side of the Throne, and it is called the “Spirit proceeding from the divine Command.” Its Spirit is the source of all spirits, represented by yellow light, the lower pillar on the right. Its Soul is the source of all souls, represented by green light, the upper pillar on the left. Its Nature is the source of all natures, represented by red light, the lower pillar on the left.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01239
The worlds are thus arranged in five levels:
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01240
The world of Divinity (lahut), or the “world of secrets” ('alam al-asrar): the Unrevealed, the realm of the active divine Command (amr fi'li).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01241
The world of Lights, or pure Intelligences ('alam al-anwar): the world of jabarut, represented by white light.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01242
The world of Spirits ('alam al-arwah): the higher malakut, represented by yellow light.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01243
The world of Souls: the lower malakut, represented by green light. The imaginal world ('alam al-mithal, mundus imaginalis) is the world of Images belonging to the whole malakut.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01244
The world of material bodies, or Nature, represented by red light.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01245

The four lights that first shine from the Light of Lights—the primordial Muhammadan Reality—are also the archangels who did not have to bow before Adam (see Qur'an 2:32). They did not bow because they were the lights before which the other angels bowed when they bowed before Adam. Some texts also speak of fourteen higher archangelic lights shining from the Light of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. These, too, did not bow to Adam: together they formed the luminous being of the heavenly Human. Earlier (p. 55), we suggested a possible comparison with the fourteen Aeons of light mentioned in certain Coptic Gnostic texts.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01246

What does this image of the Throne mean for a living person? In Shiite spirituality, the faithful believer, one who follows the path fully (mu'min), has a spiritual being made up of rays from the Throne's four lights. Every individual existence receives the very act of existing from the reality symbolized by white light; its distinct identity from yellow; its particular form and measure from green; and its original matter from red.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01247

A saying expresses this mystery of the Muhammadan Reality as the source of all realities and essences: “I am the Essence of essences (dhat al-dhawat). I am the Essence of everything that has an essence” (of all the ways Essence takes form, al-dhawat li'l-dhat). This is also what Shiite thinkers such as Mulla Sadra explain when commenting on the Throne.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01248

Shaykh Ahmad Ahsa'i sums up the overall structure of existence in this way. The first existence, brought directly into being by the divine Command and receiving that Command within itself (amr maf'uli), is the primordial body of the Light of Lights. It is one Light with fourteen flames: the “fourteen temples of God's oneness” (tawhid). Together they form one primordial essence. From it radiates the light of the cherubic Intelligences, the “Angels of the Veil,” and the light from which the prophets were created. The beings of faithful believers were in turn created from the light radiating from the prophets, and so on down to the earth itself.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01249

He writes: “Nothing is created from an essence lower than itself. Every lower reality is created from the light radiating from a higher reality. A higher reality is, for example, the sun itself; a lower reality is the sunlight that falls upon the surface of the earth. Every reality possesses its true nature (haqiqat) at its own level and in relation to what stands below it. But in relation to what stands above it, it is a symbol and image (majaz), something brought into effect.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01250

Here two ways of understanding the Book come together: the Book of the World (Liber mundi), the cosmic Qur'an, and the Book of Revelation (Liber revelatus). At the same time, the whole complex practice of ta'wil—reading symbols to discover their inner meaning—becomes rooted in the very process by which things come into existence.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01251

For in each of the worlds described above, worlds that can only be indicated by symbols (and here we should be quite clear about the difference between a symbol and an allegory), the prophetic Word passes through another stage of its descent. The Word gradually takes on a more definite form until it becomes the written Book. These are the successive ways in which the eternal Qur'an appears as it passes from world to world.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01252

At the level of lahut, the realm of Divinity and the Unrevealed, the “world of secrets” ('alam al-asrar), there is not yet any Word (kalam), any Name, or any description. This is the first spiritual level described earlier as the “secret still wrapped in the secret.” Shiite interpretation connects it with this verse: “You did not know what the Book was, nor what faith was.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01253

“Yet We made it a light by which We guide whom We please” (42:52). It is the unfathomable depth from which the command that brings being into existence arises eternally. The being called forth by this Command is the Muhammadan Reality itself. Its Intelligence, the primordial Intelligence, is the prophetic Word: the Prophet's Word existing before time. Hence the saying, “The first thing God created was my Intelligence.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01254

This Word is both God's knowledge of creation and God's knowledge of himself in that Word. That knowledge is the eternal original of the Book (Umm al-Kitab): the Qur'an in all its appearances, levels, descents, and meanings. “We communicated to you a Spirit proceeding from Our Command. You did not know what the Book was...” (42:52). The same idea is expressed in another way: “The Qur'an is a secret sign (ramz), a message in code, between the Friend and the Beloved. No one but those two knows the true reality (haqiqat) of what it says.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01255

Divine revelation through the prophetic Word therefore begins below the level of the “secret forever wrapped in the secret,” in the world of Lights radiating from the Muhammadan Reality. This world of Lights, or pure Intelligences, is the first world to which the Prophet, in his existence before time, is sent on his mission. It marks his first “descent.” In keeping with the symbolism just described, the Qur'an is white light in this world, shining like the “White Pearl.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01256

As the act of creation moves from one world to the next, the prophetic Word is sent to the inhabitants of each higher world in turn, to announce the message to them. The eternal Qur'an “descends” (tanazzul) with him: to the world of Spirits, where it is yellow light; to the world of Souls, where it is green light, like an emerald, and where the covenant with earthly humanity takes place in the sacred history before time (Qur'an 7:171); and finally to the world of bodies, where it is red light.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01257

One basic law governs these successive manifestations. As the Word descends from one world to the next, what was openly visible—the outward meaning (zahir)—to the beings of the higher world becomes hidden, the inner meaning (batin), for those of the world immediately below. At every step, a new covering or veil, symbolized by that world's colour, encloses the one before it. What was directly visible to the beings of the higher world is now a “hidden secret” in the next.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01258

Prophetic revelation as we know it on earth—with its outward and inner meanings, and with prophecy and the Imams as its two inseparable sides—has had this same structure from the very beginning of the worlds through which it passes. We know, too, that the inner meaning of prophetic revelation in every world is the inner reality of the primordial Muhammadan Reality: the complete spiritual company of the Twelve Imams, the “place of the prophetic message.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01259
The beings of the world of Lights have their own powers of perception and understanding (masha'ir), formed from the light overflowing from the Muhammadan Reality.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01260

Yet even they do not understand the Qur'an as the Prophet-Word understands it at that level beyond time. Likewise, what the beings of the world of Souls understand as a hidden meaning is only an outward covering, a husk (qishr), compared with what the beings of the world of Spirits know.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01261

What is hidden knowledge in the world of Spirits is still only a husk beside what the pure Intelligences of the world of Lights know. And even those Intelligences grasp no more than a husk compared with the knowledge of the Prophet-Word.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01262

So the hidden meaning reached by the beings of the world of Souls is only a “husk of a husk” beside the Prophet-Word's knowledge of the original Qur'an, the Muhammadan Reality itself. At the lowest level, those in our world who read only the literal words reach merely the outer husk of what readers seeking the inner meaning can perceive. This is why, for these thinkers, the haqiqat discovered through inner interpretation is not an allegorical truth. It is a spiritual truth that is literally real at its own level: spiritual because it belongs to a higher world, and literal because it matches the way things exist and are perceived in that world.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01263

When sayings speak of an inner meaning known only to prophets and Imams, they mean the innermost meaning in its absolute reality. What counts as hidden for us on earth is still outward and visible to beings above us. But the absolute inner meaning, which is not and can never become an outward meaning, belongs to the Fourteen Immaculate Ones alone.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01264

When this descent of the Qur'an reaches our earthly world, the world of things perceived by the senses, it begins the cycle of prophecy. That cycle starts with Adam and continues from prophet to prophet until the Muhammadan Light appears in full in the “Seal of the Prophets,” the last prophet to bring a divine law. Each earlier prophet had been a partial appearance of that Light. With Muhammad's revelation, the cycle of prophecy closes and the cycle of walayat—the spiritual guardianship of the Imams—begins (see Chapter VI). It starts with the First Imam and will end with the return of the Twelfth Imam, bringing our age to its close (see Book VII).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01265

As we have just seen, the way the Word passes from one world to another requires the presence of the Imams on earth once the Word has become a Book. Imam and Book belong together. A saying often repeated in Shiite circles puts it neatly: “The Qur'an is the silent Imam. The Imam is the speaking Qur'an.” At the end of its descent, the Word has become a Book made of written words, accounts, and stories—hikayat.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01266

As we noted earlier, this Arabic term suggests something important: the events of a story told on earth do not contain their full meaning in themselves. They resemble, or correspond to, events that have taken place or are still taking place in higher worlds, and those higher events give them meaning. This is what I mean by sacred history—a history whose meaning lies beyond ordinary earthly events.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01267

To understand it is to practise ta'wil. Revelation has completed its descent (tanzil); now we must lead the Book back to its source, its original form. The whole movement has two arcs: an arc of descent (nuzul, tanzil), representing the prophetic mission that brings revelation down, and an arc of return (su'ud), the arc of the Imams, which carries out ta'wil by retracing the path of descent in the opposite direction.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01268

This vision of existence helps us understand statements by these writers that would otherwise be puzzling. They say that the books revealed to earlier prophets—the Torah, Psalms, and Gospel—are all versions of the Qur'an, different states in which it appears; the Qur'an is their secret, their living core, and their deepest meaning is contained within it. That is why the Imam of the Resurrection (Qa'im al-Qiyamat) will reveal the secret of every divine revelation through complete ta'wil.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01269

They also say that the Qur'an contains knowledge of the “world of Mysteries” beyond the senses: events that took place in other worlds or will take place in ours; teachings that reached us and teachings that did not; truths kept hidden among the prophets, the Near Angels, the Cherubim, and the highest angels; and all the intimate prayers and psalms (munajat) spoken by a prophet, an Imam, or an angel.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01270
Looking out over this immense horizon, Sayyed Kazem Reshti writes:
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01271

My brother, read the Qur'an, and never abandon it. It is more precious to you than anything else. If you persevere, you will see the secret of what I have just said. When you understand these things, you will have gained a certain measure of knowledge of the Qur'an.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01272

But you will also understand that you cannot read it as it truly is. That is beyond us, whether as Muslims (muslimin) or as believers (mu'minin). Only the prophets and the Imams can read it in that way [...].
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01273

Do not let the little understanding you possess mislead you into claiming that you know the Qur'an. So do not turn against someone who makes a claim and supports it from the Qur'an in a way different from your own understanding, provided you find nothing in that person's reading that is ruled out or contradicted by the sayings of the Imams and the agreement of the true School, the Imami tradition [...].
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01274

Once you understand that the Qur'an's true meaning, its spiritual reality (haqiqat), is a coded message (ramz) understood only by God Most High, the Prophet, and the members of his Household—the Twelve Imams—and that the members of that Household share it with those who make their home among them, you will understand something else. We hear the Qur'an from the Prophet in many worlds, and at last we understand, as far as we are able, what has filtered through to this world. These many worlds differ in their subtlety and obscurity, their height and density, their freedom from matter and their materiality.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01275
We must therefore recognize that our understanding varies with the different powers by which we understand.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01276

Starting from the lowest level of manifestation, where the Qur'an appears as a Book, we can trace these different depths. When we understand it only after its descent to the world of bodies, symbolized by red light, and perceive no more than its outermost husk, we are dealing with its outward meaning (zahir).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01277

What we understand of it in the imaginal world (mundus imaginalis)—the world of the “emerald cities,” Jabalqa, Jabarsa, and Hurqalya, the world of Images within the malakut—is called its inner meaning (batin). What we understand in the malakut, the world of Souls symbolized by green light, is the inner meaning of the inner meaning (batin al-batin). In the world of Spirits, represented by yellow light, we reach the inner meaning of the inner meaning of the inner meaning. And in the world of pure Lights, represented by white light, we reach a fourth depth of inner meaning.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01278
Divine mercy comes closer to us as it lifts us to higher knowledge. In the words of a sacred saying (hadith qudsi), “My love has no limit and no end.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01279

Yet our author reminds us that everything we can understand is still only an outward meaning, a husk, compared with the first spiritual realities from which our own existence proceeds. In other words, even what we perceive as the deepest inner meaning is outward and visible compared with the being and understanding of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. Our intelligence—the subtlest part of ourselves—is to their being what a body is to a spirit.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01280

If our own speech can be expressed on the levels of Intelligence, Spirit, Soul, Image, and body, we can begin to imagine what a different order of speech belongs to them at each level or “dwelling place” through which they appear as they descend from world to world.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01281

This is simply the same law of manifestation applied to ourselves. As we have seen, what is outwardly manifest at a higher level becomes hidden at the level below, as though successive veils were being added. Or we may think of existence becoming increasingly receptive to, and dependent upon, the Command that brings it into being, until that Command makes it a being in this world—and makes the Word a Book. The levels at which we interpret the revealed Book match the levels at which being itself is revealed, as the cosmic Qur'an, from the first Command.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01282

The two-part saying of the Sixth Imam quoted at the beginning of this chapter can therefore be understood in both directions. Earlier we explained it by tracing the descent of the primordial Muhammadan Reality.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01283

We can now understand it through the hierarchy of worlds and the corresponding levels of Qur'anic interpretation, following the return upwards, in the opposite direction. In the descending order, the inner meaning is first the “secret still wrapped in the secret,” compared with what appears in the world of pure Lights. It is next the “secret beyond a secret”: the secret of the first manifestation of God as the Muhammadan Reality, which encloses the secret of the Unrevealed, compared with what appears in the world of Spirits. It is then the secret hidden beneath the outward appearance in the imaginal world, “the secret that only a secret can teach,” for the world of Souls.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01284
Finally, it is the secret concealed beneath the outward forms perceived by human beings in the earthly world. These are the four spiritual levels (maqamat) described earlier.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01285

Knowing the Qur'an, in this sense, means coming to know the secret of God's oneness (tawhid) as it appears through the Fourteen Immaculate Ones. It is an immense and demanding undertaking. This is why the Imams repeatedly said: “Our cause is difficult and demands great effort. Only an Angel brought close to God, a prophet sent with a mission (nabi mursal), or a believer whose heart God has tested in faith can bear it.”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
en-book-1-ch-5-s3
3. Reading the Qur'an for Its Hidden Meaning
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01286

We cannot go into every method used in this highest form of interpretation. Let us recall the distinction between two terms. By hermeneutics I mean the way understanding works: how someone understands something according to their own way of existing, and how they can make that understanding clear to someone else. Exegesis refers more specifically to the detailed work of explaining a text—the practical methods through which interpretation is carried out. The treatises that discuss these questions systematically are extremely complex. They offer several overlapping arrangements of levels of meaning. One day these should be compared with the methods of Jewish Kabbalah and Christian esoteric thinkers.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01287

In general, the distinction between outward meaning (zahir) and inner meaning (batin) corresponds to the distinction between tafsir and ta'wil. Tafsir explains the Qur'an as its words appear in their direct, literal sense. It follows the rules of Arabic grammar, uses the meanings recorded in dictionaries, and allows figurative meanings when the passage requires them. It draws on history, law, language, and poetry to resolve difficulties in the written text.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01288

Great works of tafsir have been produced in classical Arabic and Persian by commentators known as mufassirun. Those who seek the inner meaning have never denied the value of this work at the level where it belongs: the level of understanding the text as it appears to ordinary reading. Unfortunately, we cannot say that every commentator has shown the same openness towards the possibility of another way of reading. There is no need to reopen that argument here.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01289

We have already noted that ta'wil means literally to bring something back to its origin, to its original pattern or source (asl). For example, it leads each hikayat, each story, back to the event beyond ordinary history that it reflects and expresses in historical form. In its broadest sense, ta'wil can describe every form and level of interpretation that seeks an inner meaning, including all the successive depths of batin we have just described.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01290

But the practice varies considerably. The differences depend on what a thinker believes about being and the beings that exist, and therefore on what that thinker understands revelation to mean. Averroes does not practise ta'wil in the same way as the Ismailis, Twelver Shiites, Illuminationist philosophers, or Sufis such as Ruzbihan. These different approaches need not contradict each other. Their levels of interpretation are not opposing sides in a contest.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01291

Sometimes tafsir itself is used in such a broad sense that it includes ta'wil. For example, Mulla Sadra Shirazi's monumental work is called a Tafsir, although it is really an exercise in ta'wil. The reverse also happens. As Sayyed Kazem points out, ta'wil can have a narrower meaning than the one just described. In that case it names a kind of interpretation lying between the outward meaning (zahir) and the higher levels of inner meaning (batin).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01292

Used in this narrower sense, ta'wil connects the Qur'anic text either with the small world within us—the human being understood as a miniature universe, where Qur'anic teachings illuminate our inner life, as in Semnani's interpretation discussed later—or with the alchemical process and all its spiritual implications. The latter concerns the intermediate human being (al-insan al-awsat), between the natural person and the Perfect Human, or what Arabic writers call al-mawlud al-falsafi, the being the Latin alchemists called the Filius philosophorum, the “child of the philosophers.” Here ta'wil brings the Qur'an to life at the level of earthly human existence and the changes a person undergoes inwardly.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01293

Going beyond this, into the higher levels belonging to worlds beyond the senses—the spiritual stages described earlier, and the ways the Fourteen Immaculate Ones or the Muhammadan Reality exist at different levels of manifestation—is called tafhīm batini, a higher form of inner interpretation.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01294

Has anyone actually carried out this kind of interpretation systematically for the entire Qur'an? As far as I know, not completely. Many scholars have attempted it, however, and some have achieved part of the task. A complete treatment would exceed the strength and lifespan of one person. It would take a team of scholars, or several lifetimes of work, and the result would fill several library shelves. Its starting point must remain the sayings and teachings (hadith) of the Shiite Imams, who themselves set out the principles behind the Qur'an's many levels of meaning.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01295

We should not be surprised that Twelver Shiites, who often had to keep their beliefs and activities hidden during Islam's early centuries, were already fully occupied with preserving as many of the Imams' teachings as they could. Only later could scholars begin to organize those teachings into a larger system.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01296

Today we have substantial commentaries called tafsir—though many are really works of ta'wil—that collect, beside each Qur'anic verse, the sayings in which an Imam explains or refers to that verse. Some have been published; other major works remain unfinished or unpublished. The Shaykhi school has produced exemplary commentaries on several chapters of the Qur'an.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01297

Ismaili thinkers, for their part, have generally preferred to weave their interpretations into large works that set out a complete system of thought. Nor could we study this subject properly without the commentaries of Sufi spiritual thinkers such as Ruzbihan—who draws on earlier Sufi commentaries—Ibn Arabi, and Semnani. Their approaches often meet or overlap. Taken together, these works open up the wide horizons of spiritual interpretation that we discussed earlier (Chapter IV).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01298

For Shiite spiritual thinkers, reading the Qur'an alongside the teachings given by the Imams to their close companions and disciples is the central practice of meditation. This is why a Western reader who knows the Qur'an only through a grammatically accurate, literal translation into a European language cannot begin to imagine everything that a spiritually trained Muslim reader finds there. Such a reader cannot fully understand Sayyed Kazem Reshti's appeal quoted above (p. 209), or the many similar appeals. In the West we have never had the opportunity to read the Qur'an as these sages (hukama) and seekers of spiritual knowledge ('urafa) read it. A translation that tried to communicate their experience would require immense labour and would become a very large work indeed.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01299
Someone will object that what we need instead is sound, evidence-based historical criticism. That is a legitimate approach, and we have already discussed it.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01300

But our concern here is with a fact of spiritual life that cannot be denied: the way leading Muslim spiritual thinkers have read and lived by the sacred Book for almost fourteen centuries. Spiritual experience does not make historical criticism unnecessary. Equally, however, historical criticism cannot erase the fact that people have had those experiences. If Shiite believers receive a saying as coming from an Imam, to understand that saying is to understand how it comes from the Imam for those believers. That is the question that the study of religious experience must ask, because only then can it encounter the experience as it is lived.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01301
Historical criticism may begin by arguing, on its own grounds, that a particular text cannot genuinely come from the Imam. It has every right to do so within its own method.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01302

But if it starts there, it can never reach the spiritual fact we are trying to understand: it has already set aside the relation to the Imam that gives the text its meaning for the believer. It is precisely that spiritual reality that we want to grasp when we study Shiite ways of reading the Qur'an.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01303

We would therefore be mistaken to decide in advance that ta'wil, the search for hidden meaning, is nothing but a made-up technique or a flight of fancy. Literal interpretation is not the only approach that demands care and discipline. Discipline does not rule out inspiration: there can be inspired rigour and rigorous inspiration. As Sayyed Kazem Reshti writes:
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01304

God allows these levels and degrees of understanding (maqamat) to be explained only on condition that they remain secret within hearts, wrapped in the veils of mysteries. For created beings must first pass through the second ascent and then through the stage of coagulation. The stages we are speaking about lie beyond these: the stage of union through fusion, and the vision of things through the secret of the heart, through awareness beyond ordinary consciousness.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01305

Where are the Pleiades, that a human hand could reach them? If we tried to explain these stages using the language of people who accept only the visible evidence of material worlds, we would never even reach the questions involved. For here we are dealing with the secret that only a secret can teach—the very words of the saying quoted earlier (p. 189).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01306

As long as we confuse a symbol with an allegory, and assume that the realities in question could simply be known in some other way, we shall miss the point. The four lights of the Throne are not an allegory. They are a ramz: a sign in code that we can go on deciphering without ever reaching the end. It both reveals and conceals a truth that the human mind can receive only in symbolic form. People who regard spiritual worlds as nothing but abstractions will reject that truth.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01307
Yet, in the language of this tradition, only prophets can restore sight to hearts that are blind.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01308

It is understandable that scholars interpreting ancient texts should be fascinated by the remarkable archaeological discoveries of our day, discoveries that no one could have expected a generation ago.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01309

But there is no conflict between archaeology and the interpretation of hidden spiritual meanings. Nor does the first make the second unnecessary. They ask different questions because they work at different levels of understanding: their maqam, or standpoint, is different. A document that provides decisive evidence for a historian may be, for a believer seeking inner meaning, another coded sign still waiting to be understood.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01310

What the study of spiritual meaning is looking for cannot be reached simply by going ever farther back in time—not even into the immense timescales used by prehistory and the study of ancient life. Events from the earliest stages of earthly history are not, simply for that reason, events beyond history. Such events do not belong to the past tense of our ordinary speech. They unfold in worlds that can be approached only through the “secret of the heart.” This journey reaches towards the deepest horizon, where the secret of God's oneness (tawhid) appears as the secret of being itself: being eternally brought forth by its own Command, the “Be!” (Esto, KN) through which existence first appears in the First Being, the Light of Lights, shining in the fourteen radiant forms of the Immaculate Ones.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01311

Human intelligence can reach only this Manifestation, where being has already been brought into existence as something that exists. The solitary divine source that commands being into existence remains beyond the existence it creates.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01312

We can approach that source only through the manifestation that is its very Command, where being receives within itself the act that brings it into existence (amr maf'uli). This is the secret of the Imam expressed in the two-part saying quoted at the start of this chapter (p. 188).
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01313

The Twelve Imams, united in their essence as the “place of the prophetic message,” form, in their complete existence beyond time, the point where the active Command and the Command received coincide: the transcendent “Be!” (KN) and being (wujud) as it is present in an existing thing (mawjud). Shiite spirituality therefore teaches that without the Imam a human being could not truly affirm God's oneness (tawhid). The attempt would either lose God in empty abstraction (ta'til) or dissolve the difference between God and creation in the intoxication of likening them to one another (tashbih), perhaps going so far as to speak as God in the first person: Ana'l-Haqq—“I am God!”
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01314

The Imam is both the farthest horizon of the first divine manifestation and the form through which God becomes personally known: an inner companion, an unseen personal guide. We shall try to explain this more fully in Chapter VII.
V. The Inner Meaning and the Art of Interpretation
passage-en-01315

The primordial Muhammadan Reality appears level by level as a descent of both the “Book of Being” and the “revealed Holy Book.” In that descent, the Word becomes a Book. When it reaches our earthly world, the cycle of prophecy begins with Adam and continues until the appearance of the one called the “Seal of Prophecy.” The end of the prophetic cycle is also the beginning of the cycle of walayat, spiritual guardianship, which will last until the return of the Imam who is now hidden. These brief reflections on being and on the primordial Muhammadan Reality—the complete spiritual company of the Fourteen Immaculate Ones—are therefore a necessary introduction to understanding Shiite teachings about the prophets and the Imams.

We may now be in a better position to explore the Shiite teaching about prophets and Imams in detail, and to fill out the brief outline given earlier in Chapter II. So far, we have considered these matters in their full reality: in their polar dimension, where they have an unchanging source at the summit of the world of jabarut, the spiritual realm of divine power, and where everything exists together in an eternal present.
